newsitem.title: CUBA: Cubans to crack down on rentals to foreigners.
newsitem.headline: Cubans to crack down on rentals to foreigners.

text.p: The Cuban government is studying measures to crack down on rentals to tourists and other foreigners, according to a published report.

Manuel Millares, Minister of Finances and Prices, was quoted in Sunday's Juventud Rebelde as saying, "No nation permits visiting foreigners to rent in private homes without control since there is a risk to the family of cohabiting with drug traffickers, a pimp or a counterfeiter".
Millares said that measures were being studied "to preserve discipline, order and the security of the country and to avoid incurring in vices and crime with internal connotations."

Cuban law does not sanction room or apartment rentals or bed and breakfast establishments. But thousands of foreign visitors choose to live in less costly private homes rather than in the hotels run by the Cuban government or mixed Cuban-foreign enterprises.
The newspaper reported that about twenty percent of the tourists who visited Cuba during the first quarter stayed in rooms or apartments rented by their owners.
Room rentals in private homes cost between twenty and thirty dollars a night while most hotels charge from fifty to a hundred dollars.

Millares spoke at a meeting of the National Housing Institute which discussed the modification of the existing 1988 housing law and "the regulation of who has the right to rent...", the newspaper said.
"Private rentals cannot have profit-making purposes of a commercial, industrial or service character and strict control will be imposed over the client," the article said.

According to Cuban sources, the rental of rooms in private homes will be legalized with certain exceptions, but home owners will be required to receive permission from the government and to pay a substantial tax. At present, they pay no taxes on their property or rentals.
Cuban president Fidel Castro has expressed his fear that a new class of rich entrepeneurs could arise and undermine the revolution's egalitarian society.

Real estate speculation of any kind was outlawed by the revolutionary government over three and a half decades ago. The Urban Reform Law nationalized all real estate on the island, except private homes in which the owners lived.

Each of the housing units was valued according to its age, size, quality and location. When the cumulative monthly payments reached the value of the property, ownership was deeded to the family, which was no longer required to pay rent. Eighty percent of Cuban families are home or apartment owners.
